scenes.narration: Ask around and the answers point in opposite directions, from enormous multiples to slower than before. So set the loudest answers aside, look at the studies that measured programmers at work, and ask what each one actually measured.

scenes.narration: On the Lex Fridman Podcast, DHH described "that magical 10X, 100X, in a few rare cases, 1000X productivity boost", and said that to get it you have to work with the AI agents directly.

scenes.purpose: The loudest pessimistic answer, as repeated by commentary channels.

scenes.direction: Hard cut from sc03 so the two quotes read as opposites.
scenes.narration: From the other side, a run of videos and posts repeats one trial's result, in the words of the channel Macro Lens: when experienced developers were allowed AI tools, "they were 19% slower than when they weren't".

scenes.purpose: The large field experiments: a real but modest gain in output.

visual.description: One big tile: 26.08% productivity increase, label beneath. Holds through the authors' caveat.

chart.title: Field experiments at three companies

points.label: Productivity increase with an AI code suggestion tool

chart.note: Measured as output, not time saved; standard error 10.3%.

citations.label: Cui, Demirer et al., Copilot field experiments

scenes.narration: One set of field experiments followed almost five thousand software developers at three companies, in their regular jobs and partly over years, and estimated that an AI code suggestion tool raised their productivity, measured by their output, by about 26 percent. The authors note that this is substantially smaller than an earlier lab result, and suggest why: some kinds of coding are less readily helped by the tool, and coding is only part of a developer's job.

scenes.purpose: A second trial lands nearby but is less certain.

visual.description: One tile: roughly 21% increase in development speed, drawn dimmed with a 'not significant' tag.

chart.title: Google trial

points.label: Increase in development speed attributable to AI

chart.note: Did not meet the usual bar for statistical significance.

scenes.narration: A separate trial estimated a roughly 21 percent increase in development speed attributable to AI, but that estimate missed the usual bar for statistical significance, so it is less certain than it sounds.

scenes.direction: Each tile lands as its number is spoken; hold through the tools sentence.
scenes.narration: METR ran a randomized controlled trial with 16 experienced open-source developers on 246 tasks in mature projects they had worked on for an average of 5 years, randomly allowing or disallowing AI tools task by task. The tools were the February to June 2025 frontier: mostly the Cursor Pro editor with Claude 3.5 and 3.7 Sonnet.

scenes.purpose: The result: slower with AI.

scenes.narration: With AI allowed, tasks took 19 percent longer to complete.

scenes.narration: The researchers' hypothesis for why AI helped less than in earlier trials: their projects averaged about 10 years old and more than 1,100,000 lines of code, compared with the more greenfield projects in those trials.

scenes.narration: Its new raw numbers lean the same way: tasks took an estimated 18 percent less time for returning developers and 4 percent less for new recruits, but both ranges still stretch to a slowdown.

scenes.purpose: Why METR calls its new data very weak evidence.

scenes.direction: Highlight on 'decline to take part'; hold 0.5 s.
scenes.narration: And METR calls this only very weak evidence: more developers now decline to take part because they don't want to work without AI, which likely pushes its speedup estimate down, so the ones left are not a fair sample.

scenes.purpose: The largest figures so far, and why they are still far below ten times.

visual.description: Two tiles: +50% self-reported productivity gain, 67% more merged pull requests per engineer per day.

chart.title: Anthropic's report on its own staff

points.label: Merged pull requests per engineer per day

chart.note: Self-report and a count of merged changes, not measured time saved.

citations.label: Anthropic, How AI is transforming work at Anthropic

scenes.direction: Tiles land on '50 percent' and '67 percent'; tiles shrink on 'an order of magnitude below'.
scenes.narration: The largest figures so far come from Anthropic's own report on its staff: employees self-reported that they now get a 50 percent productivity gain from Claude on average, and merged pull requests per engineer per day rose 67 percent when its engineering org adopted Claude Code. A count of merged changes is not the same as time saved, but even taken at face value, both figures are an order of magnitude below ten times.

scenes.purpose: Answer the first question.

visual.description: Two lines build one per sentence.

citations.label: Cui, Demirer et al.; Google trial

scenes.direction: Line one on 'modest', line two on 'slower'.
scenes.narration: So, how much faster? In the workplace studies, with the tools they tested, the measured gains were modest, nowhere near the multiples in the hype. For experienced developers in big, mature projects they knew well, early-2025 tools made them slower, and whether today's tools have reversed that, METR's own newer data is too weak to say.

scenes.narration: But that slowdown trial holds a stranger detail, and it is about what the developers believed was happening.

onScreenText: How much time does AI save you?

scenes.narration: Take a second and make your own guess: how much time does AI save you?

scenes.purpose: Everyone predicted a speedup in the trial that measured a slowdown.

visual.description: Horizontal bars of predicted time saved, building one per group as named.

chart.title: Predicted cut in completion time, METR trial
chart.note: Measured: tasks took 19% longer with AI.

scenes.direction: Bars build as each group is named; camera punches on 'taking longer'.
scenes.narration: Before starting, the METR developers forecast that allowing AI would cut their completion time by 24 percent. After the study, with the work behind them, they estimated it had cut their time by 20 percent, in the same trial that measured them taking longer. Outside experts did no better: economists predicted 39 percent shorter completion times, and machine learning experts 38 percent.

scenes.narration: In an earlier randomized trial of Copilot, a lab task on a greenfield-style project, the measured productivity gain was 55.8 percent, yet participants in both the AI and the control group estimated 35 percent on average: they underestimated it.

scenes.purpose: Name the pattern: guesses missed both ways.

visual.description: Title card.

citations.label: Peng et al., Copilot randomized trial

scenes.narration: So the same kind of guess missed in opposite directions: too high for experienced developers in big projects they knew well, too low on a fresh task in the lab.

scenes.purpose: METR's own warning that self-reported speedups are unreliable.

visual.description: The METR 2026 passage with the unreliability clause highlighted.

excerpt.highlight: those estimates can be quite unreliable

scenes.narration: METR's later update adds that some developers now self-report very high speedups, and repeats that, as its earlier study found, such estimates can be quite unreliable.

visual.description: Title card.

scenes.narration: So can developers tell? In both of these trials, not reliably: their guesses missed by a wide margin.

scenes.purpose: Close: every number has a context; measure for yourself.

visual.description: Two lines build one per sentence.
onScreenText: Particular people, particular work, particular tools

scenes.direction: Second line on 'ask what they measured'; hold 1.5 s at the end.
scenes.narration: Every number in this video belongs to particular people, doing particular work, with particular tools. So when someone tells you how much faster AI makes them, ask what they measured, and if you want to know for yourself, time comparable tasks with the tool and without it rather than trusting the feeling.
